item.title: 'Non-lethal': How India and Israel's brutal use of pellet guns spread worldwide. [ middleeasteye ]
item.description:
'Non-lethal': How India and Israel's brutal use of pellet guns spread worldwide

Submitted by Anuradha Bhasin on Wed, 09/23/2026 - 11:36
The real danger isn't in how these lethal technologies, including pellet guns, are exported and shared; the greater peril is in the precedent their use against civilian protesters sets
Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) supporters wave national flags a day after the resignation of India's Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan in Mumbai, India, 26 July 2026 (Punit Paranjape/AFP)
On

In July 2026, Amnesty International published a report Made in India: the supply of weapons and munitions to Israel. It found India shipped hundreds of thousands of weapon parts and munitions components to Israel throughout its Gaza offensive, and it warned the exports carry a "substantial risk" of contributing to what it calls Israel's "ongoing genocide".

The real danger isn't only in how these lethal technologies are exported and shared. The greater peril is in the wrong precedent their use against civilians sets.

A telling example is the use of pellet guns by police in Delhi to control a student’s march to the Indian parliament in protest against an examination leak scam, which injured at least 10 civilians, including a young man who may lose his vision forever. 

The journey of the use of pellet guns for crowd control from Kashmir to New Delhi reminds us that any battleground is always a testing ground. What gets legitimised in one place does not stay there. 

India introduced pellet guns in 2010 in Kashmir and framed it as a "non-lethal" or "less-lethal" weapon for crowd control. Between 2010 and 2019, 24 people were killed. Most casualties happened after their widespread use to control violent protests following the death of militant commander Burhan Wani, who was killed in an encounter in 2016. Between July 2016 and February 2019, metal pellets killed 18 people, blinded 139, and resulted in 2,942 injuries, of which 1,459 were serious eye injuries. 

A pellet gun is a .12-bore pump-action shotgun, normally used in bird hunting, that fires a cartridge loaded with several hundred metal pellets that disperse over a wide area rather than travelling as a single projectile.

Each cartridge holds up to several hundred small pellets. On firing, the pellets scatter outward in a wide spray at about 100-150 metres per second. Because of this spread, one shot can strike multiple people in a crowd at once.

In short, it doesn’t choose its target. It can hit anyone within that range. The enormous scale of injuries, even deaths, caused by pellets in Kashmir and the people they hit - a girl sitting by her window, a baby in her mother’s arms - made no distinction between allegedly violent protesters and those who just happened to be in the wrong place at the wrong moment.

Opening old wounds

The brutality of the pellet guns cannot be fully comprehended without understanding how the lives of the majority of the victims are scarred forever. 

Despite the "less-lethal" tag, the pellets are sharp enough to pierce the skin and stay embedded in the body, causing permanent pain in some cases. On occasion, they have caused permanent blindness. The psychological wounds they inflict are irreparable. There have also been cases of injuries resulting in deaths. 

Yet, the use of pellet guns in Kashmir was justified under a manufactured broad consensus built entirely through a security prism. 

The state embraced the weapon, framing it as "non-lethal", despite documentary evidence of hundreds blinded, scores killed, and many others permanently disabled. It invited no uproar or outrage. This nationwide tendency to see Kashmir as a state of exception has also encouraged a shameful mocking of its victims - the latest example being the forthcoming Bollywood film Chauhaan. 

It was used with the bland justification: terrorism, national security. This, even as there is no documentary evidence of the weapon ever being used against insurgents - only on civilian protesters. A security doctrine, borrowed from international playbooks, and built for a region on the pretext of insurgency, is now being exported. 

History of violence

Before its use in Delhi, pellet guns were used during the farmers’ protest and in Manipur. Their use in Delhi against protesting students evoked nationwide outrage, with the framing "they were students, not terrorists’". That framing never extends to the community the national imagination has already conflated with terrorists - Kashmir, Manipur and Punjab (whose farmers led the protests). The presumption of innocence isn't universal. It is assigned by identity.

Lethal weapon: How Bollywood's 'Chauhaan' trivialises the suffering of Kashmiris maimed by Indian forces
Read More »

Far more problematic is the state response that is still relying on old tactics of skirting questions about pellet injuries. It has moved from denial to deflection but no accountability.

As opposition leaders led by Congress, a party that ironically introduced pellet guns in 2010, are uniting and demanding answers to who ordered the pellet guns and why, India’s home minister Amit Shah has refused to attend parliament. 

Zero accountability automatically translates to a continuum of use of pellet guns or other weapons framed as "non-lethal’". In Kashmir, there is a documented record of young men killed when tear gas shells were directly aimed at their upper bodies in 2010. 

Even the Supreme Court has refused a total ban on the use of pellet guns and has deflected the question to examining the gaps between standard operating procedures and realities on the ground. The debate on whether lethal weapons can be used for crowd control is incomplete if restricted to these issues.

The debate also needs to take into account the impact of weapons that are projected as "non-lethal" or "less-lethal" but kill people nonetheless. It needs to weigh up the fact that a bad precedent travels from one geography to another and beyond borders.

Lethal export

Pellet guns have already travelled the globe. The United Kingdom is the first known country to have deployed shotguns with rubber and plastic pellets during the Troubles, the 30-year violent conflict in Northern Ireland, and inspired the United States police to adopt similar versions of the weapon for crowd control.

Pellet guns are just another demonstration of how quickly any state learns that civilians can be treated as acceptable targets once the first wrongful justification goes unchallenged

Pellet guns, along with other so-called "non-lethal" weapons, have been used with impunity in Palestine. Whether India borrowed this method of repression from Israel or not, the list of countries now using it to target their own citizens is growing.

In Chile in 2019, 230 people lost their vision. Bangladesh used it in 2024, killing 22 student protesters and blinding 400. They were used in the recent Iran protests, with at least 74 documented cases of pellet injuries in vital parts of the body. A man’s lung was damaged by 174 pellets tightly packed inside his right chest cavity.  

The pellet guns are just another demonstration of how quickly any state learns that civilians can be treated as acceptable targets once the first wrongful justification goes unchallenged.

Nuclear strikes may be a rare exception, but there are enough examples, like the use of white phosphorous and drone air strikes that reveal a brutal truth: what is used in one place doesn’t stay there; it travels wherever the next authority wants the same cover of impunity.

item.title: Malaysia starts sending Myanmar migrants home. [ dawn ]
item.description:
Malaysia began sending back around 1,500 Myanmar nationals Tuesday, AFP journalists saw, launching a scheme rights groups say may endanger migrants by returning them to the war-torn country.

The batch is the first of 5,000 Myanmar citizens Kuala Lumpur says agreed to “voluntary” repatriation from detention centres amidst a huge uptick in anti-migrant sentiment in Malaysia.

But advocacy organisations say dire conditions in detention centres may have forced their decisions, and they could face dangerous homecomings in Myanmar where war has raged since 2021.

Neither Malaysia nor Myanmar have officially clarified the number of Rohingya in the first group, and there is concern they may be returned to a country where they face persecution rights groups say amounts to genocide.

Dozens of buses arrived under police escort on Tuesday at the Majlis Perbandaran Manjung stadium near the Lumut naval base in northwestern Malaysia, AFP correspondents saw, where the migrants were to be processed.

They will then be transported to the nearby naval base and taken to Myanmar by ship.

A Myanmar security source, requesting anonymity because they were not authorised to talk to media, said the boats are due to dock at Thanlyin Navy Base just south of Yangon around the end of this week.

Marine traffic websites showed Myanmar’s auxiliary support and hospital ship Than Lwin at anchor just outside the naval base.

Rohingya, a persecuted Muslim minority, make up two-thirds of the 190,000 Myanmar refugees and asylum seekers in Malaysia, according to the United Nations.

Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim announced in July that Myanmar had agreed to take back 5,000 members of the Rohingya.

‘Safe’ return promised

The plan was announced after authorities detained more than 100 Rohingya who had gathered outside the UN refugee agency’s office in Kuala Lumpur.

They were seeking help after being threatened with eviction from an informal settlement in northern Penang state.

They were later released after officials confirmed they held valid UN documentation.

Myanmar earlier this month pledged “safe and dignified” returns for its citizens displaced abroad, after criticism from the United Nations and rights groups.

Last week, more than 160 civil society groups in a joint statement called upon the Malaysian government to “immediately halt the deportations,” pending talks with civil organisations about the situation on the ground in Myanmar.

Anwar said he would invite Myanmar’s coup leader-turned-civilian president Min Aung Hlaing for an official visit to help expedite the repatriation process.

But the civil groups urged that “Malaysia’s engagement with the junta must not come at the expense of its own reputation and integrity.”

Malaysia’s home affairs ministry last month said 5,000 individuals will undergo voluntary repatriation as agreed by the Myanmar government.

There were 10,388 Myanmar nationals held at immigration detention depots by mid-August, the ministry said, with not all considered refugees.

Malaysia, which shelters one of Southeast Asia’s biggest refugee populations, is not a signatory to the 1951 Refugee Convention and does not formally recognise refugee status.

AFP fact-checkers have found that Rohingya refugees in Malaysia have been targeted by online disinformation campaigns that rights advocates say are fuelling xenophobia and intimidation.

Many of the Rohingya, a mostly Muslim group, escaped Myanmar during a brutal military crackdown in 2017.

Hundreds of thousands of Rohingya fled Myanmar after the offensive, which is the basis of a genocide case at the International Court of Justice.

More than 1.2 million live just over the border in Bangladesh, in the world’s largest refugee settlement, but talk of repatriations from there has yielded little progress.

item.title: Beyond the bottom line. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The Bangladesh Telecommunication Regulatory Commission (BTRC) opened its January spectrum auction, expecting the high-stakes competition typical of vital national infrastructure sales. Instead, the room fell silent.
Grameenphone acquired 10 MHz of the 700 MHz band at the base reserve price of Tk2,370 crore, Robi withdrew, while Banglalink stayed away from the bidding, leaving 10 MHz of the unsold spectrum to be assigned later to state-owned Teletalk at the same rate.
Failing to attract competition, this transaction left policy-makers with a critical question: How can such an auction dictate the pricing of an upcoming renewal cycle?
The short answer is it cannot . True market value requires viable alternatives where operators bid for expansion, not survival. Spectrum renewal offers no such luxury.
Once a mobile operator anchors its network architecture around a specific band and deploys thousands of base stations, walking away is no longer an option. A renewal price has little to do with market value; it is apparently a reflection of short-term state treasury demands colliding with an operator's inability to walk away without shutting down their business.
This structural disconnect matters as Bangladesh approaches the November renewal of spectrum in the 900 MHz, 1.8 GHz, and 2.1 GHz bands. Data from the GSMA’s 2025 study reveals that Bangladesh’s spectrum costs consume 15.7% of operators’ recurring revenues, much higher than the Asia-Pacific median of 10.4% and the global median of 7.7%.
Macroeconomic modeling suggests that cutting this economic burden to half could unlock $34 billion in cumulative economic benefits by 2035 and a 75% reduction could generate $45bn. These numbers are no prescription to slash prices; rather, they must be weighed against the state’s undeniable fiscal duty to manage a public asset.
At the same time, operators need capital for advanced radios and network upgrades. The real policy challenge is not finding an arbitrary, magic price per megahertz, but ensuring that every megahertz becomes highly productive.
Spectrum productivity is best measured by its capacity for dense urban hubs, wider coverage for rural villages, and reliable network quality during peak hours. Yet, BTRC data exposes a deep structural imbalance in our airwaves.
State-owned Teletalk holds 65.2 MHz for just 6.8 million subscribers, while Grameenphone must squeeze 84.4 million subscribers into 137.4 MHz. Serving remote terrain explains part of this gap, but not all of it.
When rigid frameworks lock spectrum in underutilized silos while urban networks suffer from congestion, the scarcity becomes artificial. Because traffic patterns shift constantly, a band that was adequate five years ago may leave one city congested today while sitting idle in another. If frequency blocks cannot move dynamically to match this shifting public demand, the consumer experience inevitably degrades, and the broader digital economy suffers.
Other nations have long recognized that draining an operator's capital through high upfront spectrum fees may starve the investments needed for network rollouts. Many have shifted toward models that trade immediate financial burdens for guaranteed socio-economic outcomes.
India addressed artificial scarcity by legalizing spectrum trading and sharing , allowing rights to move toward operators facing heavy traffic. Its framework permitted transfers subject to spectrum caps, roll-out obligations, eligibility conditions and a two-year holding period, with a 1% transfer fee.
Similarly, Austria and Colombia tied their low-band spectrum licensing directly to rural coverage, allowing operators to earn explicit fee discounts or convert coverage commitments into cash-equivalent credits. Spain and Canada chose to extend license terms or waive upfront renewal fees where operators could demonstrate minimum population coverage , giving companies the necessary breathing room to amortize massive hardware investments.
The warnings from the global markets should also be watched closely. In its multi-band auction, Pakistan cut reserve prices on legacy bands by more than 50%, yet those bands still drew no bids.
This proved that artificial benchmarks fail to create demand for spectrum that lacks commercial viability. In contrast, Vietnam demonstrates the power of flexible strategic asset pricing; after a failed 2023 auction, it slashed reserve prices by nearly 80%, separating long-term economic utility from the temptation of short-term cash extraction to rapidly achieve roughly 90% 5G coverage by early 2026.
Meanwhile, other regulatory experiments show distinct operational challenges: Austria faced ambiguity over how coverage would be measured. Colombia’s process was criticized for hiding minimum bids in advance while miscalculating rural rollout costs.
Finally, Canada’s model serves as a direct warning; its rigid obligation conditions drove up holding costs without incentivizing efficient use, creating long-term operational inefficiencies after the regulator ignored industry challenges during consultations.
To break out of the cycle of revenue-maximizing deadlocks and deteriorating network quality, Bangladesh needs a pragmatic, forward-looking approach. Rather than exhausting operator liquidity through high upfront hurdles, BTRC can incentivize infrastructure development by recalibrating its renewal fees into a more manageable, back-loaded payment timeline.
To protect the state’s interests, the time value of money can be maintained through transparent indexation, while operators preserve the vital cash flow.
Furthermore, the regulator can introduce an infrastructure offset mechanism . Operators should be allowed to discharge a defined portion of their renewal fees through verified capital investments in high-priority public infrastructure.
To ensure transparency, these projects must be selected from a pre-approved national registry, such as expanding coverage in deep rural unions, and undergo rigorous independent valuation.
This framework must carry strict non-delivery penalties and exclude any publicly subsidized projects to prevent double counting.
Crucially, these renewed licenses should mandate measurable outcomes:
Such a spectrum-for-investment bargain remains credible if the measurement framework is indisputable. Methodology, sampling, thresholds, and audit rights must be fixed before renewal.
Bangladesh has learned this the hard way; a Tk 21 crore network quality testing system deployed by the BTRC in 2022 failed to yield a conclusive public report for years simply because the regulator and operators could not agree on measurement metrics.
Fortunately, that gap is finally closing with the commission’s recent approval of a tighter, collaboratively developed drive-test protocol, which provides the necessary baseline for future enforcement.
Frequency blocks must be allowed to flow where the users essentially are. The BTRC should formalize a secondary market framework that permits operators to lease or temporarily transfer underutilized spectrum under clear competition rules.
This must be backed by a strict anti-hoarding policy. If an operator leaves an assigned band materially underused across a specific region for more than 18 months, they must deploy it against agreed performance indicators, open it for voluntary localized sharing, or surrender it back to the national pool.
This flexibility should be driven by real-time monitoring. Instead of allowing expensive auditing tools to sit idle, the regulator should leverage its updated field-testing capabilities to publish monthly, region-specific network performance reports.
Linking continued spectrum retention to these localized, busy-hour quality audits will transform transparency into an enforcement tool, forcing operators to prioritize real-world delivery over asset hoarding.
The current policy standoff is primarily behavioral -- regulators are historically evaluated on immediate treasury targets, while operators pile up spectrum to protect market share without optimizing performance.
We must redefine what institutional achievement looks like in telecommunication governance. A spectrum renewal cycle should not be evaluated by the volume of cash deposited into the treasury on day one.
Instead, its true dividends should be measured by expanded coverage, fewer dropped calls, faster internet speeds, and the seamless rollout of next-generation 5G networks.
On the corporate side, operators must be pushed to move away from vanity metrics. Total SIM card registrations tell us really nothing about actual digital utility.
Instead, the regulatory framework should compel corporations to publicly report active data users per megahertz per base station.
This simple shift forces corporate focus toward capital efficiency and network optimization rather than defensive asset hoarding.
A high spectrum price functions as a regressive tax on the end consumer, directly stalling smartphone adoption and digital literacy in underserved communities.
By lowering upfront spectrum barriers and ensuring sufficient capacity, the per-gigabyte cost for operators drops.
The regulatory framework must ensure these savings are passed down to low-income tiers through affordable, high-volume data packages tailored for students, marginal farmers, and micro-entrepreneurs.
Directing infrastructure offsets specifically toward hard-to-reach and climate-vulnerable coastal communities ensures that our digital safety net, including mobile financial services, telemedicine, and online education, becomes accessible for the whole population, rather than a privilege concentrated within a few major metropolitan centers.
By November, the thousands of telecommunication antennas stretching across Bangladesh’s skylines will point exactly where they point today. The critical question for our future is whether the licenses governing those radio frequencies will simply preserve a congested network or lay the groundwork for tomorrow's digital economy.
A cheap megahertz that remains underutilized does nothing for national development. An overpriced megahertz that depletes an operator's investment capacity behaves no differently.
The state does not hold the radio spectrum to act as a mere fee collector; it holds it in trust as a scarce public resource. The real test of the upcoming renewal cycle is not how much revenue the state collects per megahertz; it is the quality of the digital nation emerging on the ground.

item.title: Bangladesh’s 60-year energy test. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The Bay of Bengal is rarely calm. Off the coast of Cox’s Bazar, the water churns with a saline, metallic bite, where rusting hulls of floating storage units bob like corks on an endless expanse of gray.
You can smell the diesel, hear the hum of generators, and feel the oppressive weight of humidity when the grid fails. For a decade, this has been the harsh, transient reality of Bangladesh’s energy security -- a patchwork of floating FSRUs, rented by the year, vulnerable to the violent whims of cyclones.
But beneath the waves, an alternative has been proposed.
In early September 2026, Novatek Middle East presented Petrobangla with a $950 million offer for a gravity-based structure (GBS) LNG terminal. This is not a ship. This is a concrete leviathan, permanently welded to the seabed, engineered to withstand the most violent storms for 60 to 80 years.
It offers 7.5 MTPA capacity and claims to be 21% cheaper than a conventional land-based terminal. It is a beast built for an epoch, yet it sits on the desk of a government paralyzed by the politics of the present.
The GBS is a direct challenge to the status quo of energy insecurity. In international energy theory, this is the ultimate pursuit of energy security -- the physical protection of supply routes and resilient infrastructure.
FSRUs are fragile; they drift, they shut down, and they have historically knocked out hundreds of millions of cubic feet of capacity, plunging the nation into darkness. A GBS ends that cycle. It is an anchor of sovereignty in a turbulent ocean.
Yet, the silence from Dhaka is deafening. Why? Because while the leviathan waits in the water, a golden leash has already been attached to the state's neck.
Let us step back into the air-conditioned, leather-bound rooms of Washington, where the ink of a trade deal dried earlier this year. Under the banner of "Bangladesh First," the current regime signed an agreement that binds the nation to an estimated $15 billion in American energy products over 15 years, alongside a 0% tariff structure contingent on using US cotton.
This is not diplomacy; this is economic infrastructure designed to create institutional lock-in. Under neoliberal institutionalism, international agreements are designed to raise the cost of defection. We are now legally and commercially entangled in a 13-year Gunvor contract (117 cargoes at roughly $8.60/MMBtu), which bypassed open tenders and cemented a specific, expensive pricing structure into our grid.
The theory of trade dependency holds that nations bound by such agreements lose their strategic autonomy. To accept the Russian GBS, Dhaka would have to openly defy this Western pact. The price of defiance is a 19% tariff wall, diplomatic isolation, and the wrath of Washington.
The price of acceptance, however, is a structurally superior, cyclone-proof infrastructure that ensures national survival. This is the new " paternity suit " of international politics: The US deal claims ownership over our economic future.
But the true tragedy of this moment is not the geopolitical chessboard -- it is the ghost of our own neglect.
We have spent over $20 billion on LNG imports, yet less than $800 million on domestic exploration. In the classic language of the Resource Curse, we have abandoned our own endowment to fund our dependency.
We built a nation propped up by expensive, fleeting imports while our own gas fields remained trapped under the earth, waiting for state investment. The seabed GBS would finally provide a foundation, but it stands on the ruins of our own strategic failures.
This brings us to the unflinching crossroads. We have been told this government is built on "Bangladesh first." Is that a sincere doctrine, or is it a hollow slogan to be discarded when the tariff threats begin?
We must draw a line in the sand. The Bay of Bengal is not a theater for American or Russian proxy wars; it is the lifeline of a nation of 170 million people.
The GBS is not merely a Russian asset; it is an instrument of national resilience. The US trade deal is not just a commercial agreement; it is a cage that restricts our ability to make sovereign choices.
In international relations theory, we are witnessing a brutal clash between realism -- the survival of the state through physical power and durable defense -- and neoliberalism, where economic institutions dictate behaviour.
The current government is choosing the latter, trading physical resilience for bureaucratic comfort.
As the waves crash against the shores of Cox’s Bazar, indifferent to the politics of diplomats, the concrete leviathan remains a silent, waiting monument to what could have been.
The current government faces a historic test: Will they cut the golden leash, endure the short-term costs of trade disruption, and anchor Bangladesh to a century of energy sovereignty?
Or will they continue to float, rudderless, on the precarious tides of foreign dependency?
The decision defines whether "Bangladesh first" is an actual doctrine -- or just another diplomatic artifact destined for the dustbin.
Zakir Kibria is a Bangladeshi writer, policy analyst and entrepreneur based in Kathmandu, Nepal. He can be reached at zakir.kibria@gmail.com . The author previously explored these dynamics in " The Paternity Suit " for the Dhaka Tribune.

item.title: Getting tough on vandalism. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
It is extremely concerning to see multiple incidents involving vandalism, looting, and unlawful gatherings in recent days across the city, once again raising serious questions about public safety and the ability of institutions to protect property, businesses, and essential services.
The concern is not confined to any single incident or location: From attacks on private establishments to the destruction of a healthcare facility and other acts of violence and looting, the recurrence itself is what is deeply troubling.
It goes without saying: Dhaka cannot afford to normalize the kind of lawlessness that has become increasingly visible across the city.
What makes such incidents particularly alarming is the apparent ease with which groups can gather, enter premises, damage property, and remove belongings.
When vandalism becomes a repeated occurrence, it creates an environment in which ordinary citizens and businesses can no longer feel confident that their property will be protected. That is unacceptable in any functioning city.
Law enforcement agencies must therefore move beyond arresting some suspects after the damage has already been done. Investigations must identify the organizers, participants, enablers, as well as systemic failures that allowed the attacks to happen. The investigation into possible police negligence surrounding the Mirpur incident is particularly important in this regard.
At the same time, accountability cannot be selective. Political affiliation, social standing, or the nature of a dispute must not determine whether the law is enforced.
Disagreements over property, business, or other matters must be resolved through lawful institutions -- not intimidation, destruction, or force.
Dhaka already faces enormous challenges in maintaining public order and protecting its residents. Allowing vandalism and looting to recur will only deepen insecurity and erode public confidence.
The message should be clear: Disputes can be contested, grievances can be addressed, and allegations can be investigated, but no one has the right to take the law into their own hands. A safe city depends on that principle being enforced consistently.

The first quarter-final, scheduled at Korogi Sports Park, was called off at the time of the toss after incessant showers left large parts of the ground under covers. Officials determined there was no realistic chance of play, even in a heavily reduced format.

Pakistan, one of four seeded teams alongside India, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh that received a direct entry into the last eight, advanced under tournament regulations that award the higher-ranked side progression in the event of a no-result.

Hong Kong, ranked significantly lower, exited the competition without taking the field.

Hong Kong had reached the quarter-finals by finishing second in Group ‘B’ having defeated Malaysia by eight wickets before suffering a 41-run loss to Oman.

Pakistan had arrived in Japan after a training camp in Karachi and a practice session in Nisshin that was also disrupted by overnight rain and a wet outfield.

The side, captained by Sahibzada Farhan and coached by Mike Hesson, will face the winners of Tuesday’s quarter-final between Bangladesh and Malaysia in the semi-finals, scheduled for Thursday at the same venue.

This would have been the third T20 meeting between the two sides, with Pakistan having prevailed in both previous encounters at the 2022 Asia Cup and the 2023 Asian Games. Pakistan won bronze in the men’s cricket event at the 2010 Asian Games.

The second quarter-final between India and Afghanistan, scheduled to be the later fixture at the same venue was also abandoned without a ball bowled due to rain.

India, being the higher-ranked side, advanced to the semi-finals where they will meet the winners of the quarter-final between Sri Lanka and Nepal.

The semi-finals are set for October 1, with the bronze-medal match and final scheduled for October 3.

item.title: The right to know matters more than ever. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Information has never been so abundant. Yet finding information that can be trusted has rarely been more difficult.
The scale of the problem is now global. The World Economic Forum's Global Risks Report 2026 ranks misinformation and disinformation as the second most serious risk over the next two years, behind geoeconomic confrontation.
The report, based on the perceptions of more than 1,300 experts worldwide, notes that technological acceleration and the growing difficulty of distinguishing authentic from synthetic content are intensifying the challenge.
Artificial intelligence has made the problem more acute. Convincing audio, video and text can now be generated and distributed at unprecedented speed and scale. Fake news cards mimicking established media outlets can be produced within minutes, while social media systems can rapidly amplify content designed to provoke fear, anger, or polarization.
The result is not simply an increase in false information; it is a deeper crisis of trust in which distinguishing fact from fabrication becomes increasingly difficult.
The WEF report warns that realistic deepfakes and AI-generated misinformation and disinformation could further fragment the public sphere and make it increasingly difficult for citizens to distinguish truth from deception.
This year's International Day for Universal Access to Information, observed on September 28, comes against precisely this backdrop. The 2026 theme -- “Upholding Information Integrity in the Digital Age: The Role of Access to Information in Addressing Information Disorder” -- highlights the importance of access to reliable information at a time when digital technologies and artificial intelligence are making it increasingly difficult to distinguish authentic information from false or manipulated content.
In recent years, false claims about political developments, communal violence, and government decisions, fabricated press releases and AI-generated images and videos have repeatedly circulated online. Data from Dismislab and Rumor Scanner indicate that the spread of political and religious rumours in Bangladesh increased significantly in 2024 and 2025.
This phenomenon is generally discussed as a problem of misinformation or disinformation. But there is another dimension that deserves greater attention: The availability of reliable information from authoritative sources.
When citizens cannot easily find out what a public authority has decided, how public money has been spent, or what the official record actually says, an information vacuum is created. That vacuum can quickly be filled by rumours, speculation, and fabricated narratives.
This is where the Right to Information (RTI) Act, 2009 becomes particularly important.
RTI is not a fact-checking mechanism, and the Information Commission is not a fact-checking agency. Its role is different: To ensure that citizens can obtain information from authorities covered by the law, seek remedies when information is denied, and ensure compliance with the legal right to information.
But that role matters greatly in an age of information disorder. Reliable public information gives citizens something against which claims can be checked.
Consider a false claim about a government decision spreading rapidly online. One response may be to publish another statement denying it. A more durable response is to ensure that the actual decision, relevant documents, and other information are proactively available to the public. The easier it is to find the authoritative record, the less room there is for an information vacuum to be filled by falsehoods.
This makes the current state of Bangladesh's Information Commission particularly concerning.
The Commission has remained without commissioners since 2024. A five-member selection committee has been reconstituted to recommend candidates for the posts of chief information commissioner and two information commissioners. However, no subsequent appointments have been publicly reported.
The Information Commission is the institution through which citizens can ultimately seek a remedy when their requests for information are denied after the prescribed appeal process. Without commissioners, that enforcement mechanism cannot function as intended. The burden of exercising a legal right therefore falls disproportionately on the citizen.
A right is meaningful only when there is an effective mechanism for enforcing it.
Civil society organizations and research-based organisations such as Transparency International Bangladesh (TIB), along with the RTI Forum, have repeatedly called for the Commission to be made fully functional and for commissioners to be appointed through a transparent process based on competence and independence.
These demands are part of a broader reform discussion about making the right to information work effectively in practice, rather than merely guaranteeing it on paper.
But restoring the Commission alone will not resolve the weaknesses in Bangladesh's RTI regime. The law itself needs reform.
The RTI Act was an important governance reform when it was enacted in 2009. But more than 15 years later, the information environment, technology, and expectations of citizens have changed considerably. The law must therefore evolve with these realities.
The RTI (Amendment) Ordinance, 2026 introduced several important changes, including provisions recognising electronic records, stronger proactive disclosure requirements, and increased penalties for certain violations. But important concerns remained. Among them was the exclusion of official note sheets from the definition of information.
The exclusion of note sheets is significant because such records can reveal how an administrative decision was processed, considered, and justified. If citizens can obtain the final decision but not the relevant record of how that decision was reached, an important part of institutional accountability remains outside public scrutiny.
The demand to include political parties as “authorities” was also not incorporated into the ordinance.
Political parties registered with the Election Commission are not currently treated as "authorities" under the RTI Act. Although registered political parties are required to submit annual financial reports to the Election Commission, citizens cannot directly seek information from political parties under the RTI framework.
This creates a gap in public accountability. Political parties participate in elections and play a central role in determining how the state is governed. Their financial transparency is therefore a legitimate matter of public interest.
Bringing political parties within an appropriate transparency framework does not mean that every aspect of their internal affairs should automatically become public. Rather, the principle should be that organizations whose activities have significant public consequences should be subject to reasonable and clearly defined transparency obligations.
Unfortunately, these important issues were not incorporated into the ordinance.
More importantly, the ordinance itself did not become permanent law. Introduced during the interim government following the July uprising, the ordinance was not enacted into permanent law after the elected government took office.
Under Article 93 of the Constitution, an ordinance ceases to have effect if it is not enacted within the constitutionally prescribed period after Parliament begins to function.
As the 13th Parliament did not pass the RTI Amendment Ordinance into law, it lapsed. The amendments it introduced therefore did not become part of the permanent RTI framework, leaving the RTI Act 2009 as the governing law.
A reform process that had introduced significant changes to the country's information-access regime therefore went back to square one.
Important changes to citizens' right to information should not remain dependent on temporary ordinances. Bangladesh needs a durable legal framework developed through meaningful consultation with citizens, journalists, researchers, civil society, and other stakeholders.
But legal reform alone will not solve the problem of information disorder.
The government must also take proactive disclosure seriously. Public authorities should routinely publish decisions, budgets, expenditure, audit reports, project information, and other information of genuine public interest in accessible and usable formats.
This is particularly important because the technology for producing and distributing false information is evolving rapidly.
The WEF report notes that distinguishing authentic from synthetic content -- whether video, audio, or written material -- is becoming progressively more difficult, while AI-generated misinformation and disinformation can amplify existing social and political divisions.
Citizens, meanwhile, need greater awareness of their right to information and greater capacity to assess information critically.
We therefore need to think about RTI differently. It is not simply an anti-corruption tool. It is not merely a mechanism for journalists to obtain documents. And it is certainly not a substitute for professional fact-checking.
It is part of the information infrastructure of an informed society.
A citizen trying to determine whether a claim about public expenditure is true should be able to find the relevant government record.
A journalist investigating a public project should be able to seek the underlying information.
A community questioning the distribution of public benefits should have a lawful means of obtaining relevant records.
And when an authority refuses information without justification, there should be an independent institution capable of providing a remedy.
For that to happen, Bangladesh needs three things at the same time.
The appointment of information commissioners should therefore be completed through a transparent process based on competence, independence, and freedom from partisan influence or nepotism.
The law should be further reviewed to address its remaining gaps, including the treatment of note sheets and the transparency of entities whose activities have significant public consequences.
Public authorities must also comply with their existing obligations to disclose information proactively.
The right to know should not depend on how persistent a citizen is, how well connected they are, or whether they can withstand the frustration of repeatedly asking an authority for information.
In an age when convincing falsehoods can be produced and distributed within minutes, access to reliable public information is part of the foundation on which citizens make sense of public affairs.
The answer to information disorder is not simply to produce more information. It is to make reliable information accessible, verifiable and accountable.
And for that, Bangladesh must make the right to know a right that works -- not merely a right that exists on paper.
Mathews Chiran is a former journalist and now works as a communications practitioner.

item.title: The right to know. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
As a nation navigating a challenging political and economic period along with seeking to rebuild its democratic foundations, access to information must be recognized as an indispensable prerequisite for accountable governance, anti-corruption, and institutional trust.
To that end, as the global community observes the International Day for Universal Access to Information under the theme "Upholding Information Integrity in the Digital Age," we must contend with some uncomfortable truths.
Historically, Bangladesh did take a progressive step with the enactment of the Right to Information (RTI) Act in 2009. Yet, the promise of that landmark legislation has been repeatedly undermined by bureaucratic resistance, colonial-era cultures of secrecy, and prolonged periods of institutional paralysis.
In our current socio-political context, institutional secrecy breeds rumours, public cynicism, and instability. At a time when disinformation and misinformation continues to grow, and technologies only amplify their reach, it is integral for everyday citizens to be empowered with the right to know and become more informed citizens.
Indeed, if citizens are to hold the government accountable for their decisions and actions, they must first know how they are governed.
To build a truly democratic society, the state must treat the right to know as non-negotiable.Digitizing public records and ensuring unhindered access to official data for citizens are critical steps in this endeavour.
Transparency has never been a threat to effective governance, and this and subsequent administrations must recognize that it is rather the strongest defense to effective governance.
On this International Day for Universal Access to Information, we hope that the authorities concerned recognize that an informed citizenry is in its best interest, and to suppress and withhold information from the public goes against any nation’s best interests.

item.title: Fire safety cannot remain an afterthought. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Saturday’s fire on the 23rd floor of the 26-storey Ahmed Tower in Banani -- standing directly adjacent to FR Tower, where a tragic blaze claimed 26 lives in 2019 -- was brought under control by the Fire Service without casualties. This is good news, and is cause for celebration.
However, measuring urban safety solely by whether lives were lost on a single afternoon is a dangerous illusion.
Just days earlier, a horrific gas cylinder explosion at a garment factory compound in Ashulia claimed nine lives and injured dozens. Together, these incidents illustrate a chilling reality: Whether in modern commercial high-rises or sprawling industrial hubs, fire safety across Bangladesh remains a lethal afterthought.
The contrast between these two blazes exposes systemic negligence across sectors. In urban centres, rapid vertical expansion has far outpaced regulatory enforcement, with faulty electrical wiring, overloaded server rooms, unserviced air-conditioning units, and obstructed emergency exits being the norm.
In industrial corridors, unsafe handling of flammable material, improvised supply systems, and inadequate hazardous-material protocols turn factory premises into ticking time bombs for workers and nearby residents alike.
Relying on the heroic response of firefighters is not safety but a last resort. Reaching infernos above the tenth floor of a high-rise or navigating congested industrial alleys in Ashulia poses immense operational hurdles.
Thus, it is prevention, strict compliance, and active building safety systems that must form the backbone of our national fire policy.
Until building owners, industrial management, and regulatory agencies treat fire safety codes as mandatory laws rather than optional guidelines, every workplace and office tower in the country will remain a potential tragedy waiting to happen.
Those at Ahmed Tower were fortunate, while those nine in Ashulia paid the ultimate price with their lives. Fire safety must be treated with the seriousness it deserves so that citizens do not have to rely on luck to survive.

item.title: Putting a price on a life. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
On a Tuesday afternoon in Dhaka’s affluent Baridhara Diplomatic Zone, a speeding vehicle mounted the pavement and crushed 24-year-old Mehedi Hasan to death.
Mehedi was not jaywalking or dodging traffic; he was a construction worker resting on a sidewalk after long hours of manual labour.
Behind the wheel was a 17-year-old boy -- an underage driver operating a high-powered car far beyond his legal right or operational skill.
Within hours, the predictable machinery of class-based privilege creaked into motion.
Initial reports highlighted the teenager’s swift release into family custody before public outrage forced his re-arrest.
Days later came the ultimate manifestation of elite transactionality: A private financial settlement of Tk9 lakh handed to the victim’s grief-stricken family -- Tk1 lakh for funeral expenses, Tk8 lakh for his elderly parents -- in exchange for an agreement to withdraw the case and support bail.
Since this specific case remains sub judice , we cannot render a final verdict on the courtroom outcomes. Nor should we speculate on individual legal guilt.
Yet, the public spectacle of cash exchanging hands in the wake of a lost human life forces us to look in the mirror.
It exposes a deeply rooted social pathology: In our society, justice is not an unalienable right -- it is a negotiable commodity.
The Baridhara incident is not an isolated tragic error; it is the latest entry in a long, shameful history where financial muscle weaponizes the law against the powerless.
Across decades, Bangladesh’s economic elite have operated under the implicit assumption that wealth buys immunity.
In the 1990s and 2000s, political scions and industrial heirs routinely turned city streets into private racetracks.
When pedestrian fatalities occurred, the script was almost always identical: An underling or driver was substituted as the accused, local law enforcement looked the other way, and quiet payouts silenced impoverished families who lacked the financial stamina to fight long legal battles.
By the 2010s, this impunity matured from vehicular manslaughter into far more insidious territories.
The infamous 2021 case involving the tragic death of Mosarat Jahan Munia exposed how immense corporate and financial power could wrap itself in legal shields, leaving a grieving family to navigate a maze of delays and narrative manipulation.
The public watched as influence appeared to soften the sharp edges of criminal accountability.
This dynamic is hardly unique to Bangladesh. Across South Asia and the broader global landscape, wealth frequently tilts the scales of justice.
In India, high-profile hit-and-run sagas -- most notably the decades-long legal battle involving Bollywood star Salman Khan -- demonstrated how money and celebrity can stretch judicial processes over decades, exhausting victims' families until justice becomes a distant, abstract concept.
In the United States, the controversial "affluenza" defense allowed Ethan Couch -- a wealthy teenager who killed four pedestrians while driving intoxicated -- to initially escape prison time after defense attorneys argued his privileged upbringing prevented him from understanding the consequences of his actions.
Whether termed "out-of-court settlements," "compensation," or legal technicalities, the pattern remains identical: The rich kill or destroy, and money cleans up the residue.
Defenders of private settlements often argue from a pragmatic standpoint: A poor family loses its sole breadwinner, criminal trials in our region take decades, so cash offers immediate relief.
This argument is a moral trap.
To call a Tk9 lakh transaction a "voluntary settlement" between a wealthy family and a destitute one is a gross distortion of reality.
When a bereaved family facing immediate starvation takes a settlement, they are not forgiving the perpetrator; they are surrendering to their own vulnerability.
It is coercive necessity masquerading as consent.
When money is allowed to neutralize criminal accountability, the justice system effectively sets a market price on human life.
It sends a terrifying message to the working class: Your lives exist on a sliding price scale.
If a driver is wealthy enough, your death is merely an out-of-pocket expense -- a minor inconvenience resolved with a bank transfer.
If we are to break this cycle of transactional justice, our legal and social frameworks require an immediate overhaul, particularly regarding underage offenders and the ethics of mercy.
While juvenile protection laws exist to rehabilitate young offenders, they were never intended to act as a shield for gross criminal negligence.
When an underage individual takes the wheel of a heavy automobile and operates it recklessly on public roads, the act carries predictable, lethal consequences.
Treating such cases merely as minor juvenile infractions sends a message of zero consequence.
Where severe harm or death occurs, juvenile detention alone is insufficient -- there must be serious, formal legal accountability, including holding guardians legally and financially liable for enabling the crime.
Mercy is a noble element of justice, but mercy cannot be negotiated through a wire transfer.
True repentance requires accountability, remorse, and systemic restitution -- not hush money delivered before a bail hearing.
When guilt begets compensation aimed at erasing criminal charges, it ceases to be mercy and becomes corruption.
Where the formal legal system struggles against the influence of wealth, society must step in.
If the law can be slowed down or bought off, social standing must not be.
We must ask ourselves hard, introspective questions about the culture we tolerate:
It is time to turn wealth from a shield into an irrelevance when basic humanity is at stake.
The families who use money to silence the families of victims should face uncompromising social ostracization.
Their money should buy them no respect, no social invitations, and no community standing.
Until society makes it clear that wealth cannot purchase reputational immunity, the streets will remain unsafe for the poor, and the law will remain a tool that only binds those who cannot afford to buy their way out.
Wafiur Rahman looks after the business desk at Dhaka Tribune.

item.title: A global stage, a missed opportunity. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The UN General Assembly offered Prime Minister Tarique Rahman an opportunity to transcend the country’s petty political factionalism and showcase Bangladesh as a nation capable of playing a leading role on the global stage.
While this opportunity arises annually, the political transformation following the 2024 uprising lent this particular session added significance for Bangladesh.
The question now arises: Did Prime Minister Tarique Rahman make the most of this opportunity? Or did he simply follow the conventional script -- extolling his own party, vilifying opponents, and delivering a bland, bureaucratic speech on geopolitical issues that carefully avoided taking a firm stand?
It became evident right at the start of the speech that the PM would not chart a new course.
Although the nation is 55 years old, he indulged in nostalgia, recalling only the speeches delivered from that very podium by his father, the late President Ziaur Rahman, and his mother, former Prime Minister Khaleda Zia.
He could also have acknowledged that Sheikh Mujibur Rahman delivered the first-ever speech in Bangla from that same platform in 1974. Doing so would not have undermined his standing as the country’s elected representative.
Yet, no matter how grand the stage, the country’s narrow political climate leaves little room for such magnanimity.
Even when standing on the global stage, Bangladeshi leaders struggle to break free from the political divisions they leave behind at home. There have been precedents for this, and this instance was no exception.
The PM blamed the past, labelled his ousted political rivals “fascists,” and presented his party’s agenda as a blueprint for development.
It was expected that he would speak of the country’s return to the path of democracy, and it was hardly surprising that he praised the February election.
However, when the domestic practice of branding the ousted Awami League as “fascist” is exported to the global stage, it effectively amounts to painting a large segment of the nation’s population as the “enemy.”
It would have signalled a new kind of politics had he spoken solely of progress rather than portraying a fractured nation by assigning blame to others.
At one point in the speech, Prime Minister Tarique Rahman stated: “By ensuring the political and economic empowerment of the people, we aim to establish a prosperous, self-reliant, and democratic welfare state -- a nation where everyone, regardless of political affiliation, religion, or race, can live securely and safely with equal rights, honour, and dignity.”
There is no doubt that these words sound appealing to everyone.
However, it would hardly be surprising if these sentiments seemed hollow when certain party activists and supporters live in fear of arrest while facing fabricated charges, languish in prison for months without trial, or, branded as “accomplices” while being subjected to attacks, handed over to the police, and jailed on false accusations.
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman touched upon several significant issues in his speech, including migration, the impact of climate change, artificial intelligence, the Rohingya crisis, the volatile global situation, and the UN’s development goals.
In each instance, the government’s programs or achievements were highlighted. In some areas, particularly regarding the avoidance of geopolitical conflict, he advocated peace efforts and disarmament.
These are standard topics in UN politics; statements made by developing nations on these matters are often heard by others but usually forgotten before they even leave UN headquarters.
However, it is worth examining how the PM’s own publicity team is attempting to present his speech to the nation.
While briefing journalists in New York, Mahdi Amin, a spokesperson for the Prime Minister’s Office, described Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s address to the UN General Assembly as “historic and groundbreaking.”
Mahdi Amin stated that, through this speech, Bangladesh had “created a new history.”
What is this new history? Reading Amin’s remarks, it appears that he views the rare occurrence of three members of the same family addressing the UN as heads of government as the “historic” event.
It was not merely the family connection, however, but the glorification of the leader that appeared to be the government spokesperson’s primary focus.
“Through this speech, the world witnessed how a head of government transforms into a true statesman,” Amin said.
He reminded the nation that the PM did not confine himself to matters concerning Bangladesh alone, he also spoke about global peace and the rights of the freedom-seeking people of Palestine, and even offered counsel to the United Nations itself.
“He presented a concrete roadmap to world leaders on how the UN can play a robust role in restoring peace, prosperity, and unity across the globe,” Mahdi Amin said at a press conference.
There is no doubt that Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s speech touched upon these issues.
However, there is room for disagreement over whether these remarks were truly “historic” or “statesmanlike.”
First, heads of government from Bangladesh have always spoken about Palestinian rights when addressing the UN.
Nor is this unique to Bangladesh; leaders from most nations speak of peace and prosperity and express a desire to see the UN play a stronger and more effective role.
These are standard talking points for developing nations at international conferences.
Second, one could not merely disagree with, but vehemently dispute, the spokesperson’s claim that Prime Minister Tarique Rahman “presented a concrete roadmap to world leaders” on how the UN could play a robust role.
While Prime Minister Tarique Rahman certainly spoke eloquently about the UN’s role and what is expected of it, can those remarks truly be described as a “roadmap?”
The prime minister was correct in stating that, in the era of globalization, conflict in one part of the world can trigger unrest and economic disaster elsewhere.
He spoke of establishing bilateral or multilateral relations among disputing states based on “equality, fairness, mutual interest, and respect for dignity,” points with which few would disagree.
“Bangladesh envisions the UN as the focal point for establishing a cooperative global society that respects each other’s independence and sovereignty,” the PM said in his speech.
These are all fine sentiments. But where is the “roadmap” for the UN here? A roadmap would typically contain specific proposals and outline concrete steps.
These remarks are undoubtedly significant, particularly in the context of post-2024 Bangladesh-India relations. However, such sentiments are not new on the global stage, and all too often remain nothing more than rhetoric once the speech concludes.
Had the prime minister wished, he could have presented concrete proposals for reforming the UN Security Council or addressing the crisis in development funding.
Regarding the Rohingya crisis, instead of merely seeking international cooperation, he could have offered specific proposals grounded in reality; he could even have announced unilateral measures to reinforce Bangladesh’s commitment to the disarmament process.
The speech would have been truly “historic” or “groundbreaking” had it put forward proposals aimed at playing a leading role in resolving problems rather than simply positioning the nation as a victim.
As it stands, however, it appears that the address amounted to little more than a routine bureaucratic exercise of reading from prepared talking points.
Sabir Mustafa is the former head of BBC Bangla and is currently working as a freelance journalist and podcaster. Views expressed are the author’s own.

item.title: Nepal's hydropower ambitions face climate reality check. [ dawn ]
item.description:
Nepal’s hydropower boom has long been touted as a cornerstone of economic growth and renewable energy, but the devastating flood in August exposed its vulnerability.

The disaster triggered by a glacial mountain collapse on the China-Nepal border killed more than 1,400 people and left thousands missing — while knocking 410 megawatts (MW), or about 10 per cent of the generation capacity, out of Nepal’s power system.

More than 90pc of Nepal’s electricity comes from hydropower, but extensive damage to its river projects has prompted questions about its energy security as climate and geological risks intensify.

“Hydropower has been a major driving force in growth of the country… generating jobs and income,” Uttam Bhlon Lama, senior vice president of the Independent Power Producers’ Association (IPPAN), told AFP.

“It was bringing huge hope and future prospects to the people,” he said, adding that the country would now have to rethink its dam-building spree.

“We have to prepare… This is our new normal.”

Over the past decade, the Himalayan nation has increased hydropower output more than fourfold to about 4,120 megawatts, according to government figures, helping connect nearly all its 30 million people to the grid.

The country had previously moved to export surplus electricity to neighbouring India and Bangladesh, seeking to turn its glacier-fed rivers into a source of revenue. Authorities suspended electricity exports after the disaster.

The major destruction of hydropower infrastructure underscored the risks of that strategy in a region where glaciers are retreating, permafrost is thawing and extreme hazards are becoming harder to predict.

‘Serious lessons’

Nepal’s energy sector accounted for about half of the infrastructure damage from the disaster, according to government assessments.

Seven hydropower projects were directly hit while generation was halted at others, removing 410 MW from the national grid.

Six hydropower projects under construction, with a combined capacity of 508 MW, were also damaged.

Rescuers have continued searching hydropower tunnels for hundreds of missing workers, engineers and other personnel, weeks after the disaster.

The scale of the damage has prompted calls for a rethink of how projects are designed and built.

The disaster has “taught us serious lessons for the future”, Energy, Water Resources and Irrigation Minister Biraj Bhakta Shrestha told parliament on Wednesday.

“We must not only take stock of the damage but also learn from it and develop systems to reduce future risks,” he said.

The World Bank warned that Nepal needs to build a hydropower system capable of anticipating, absorbing and recovering from increasingly complex Himalayan hazards.

Scientists say the August disaster was caused by a complex chain of geological and climatic factors rather than a single extreme weather event.

According to the World Weather Attribution group, the massive rock-and-ice collapse was shaped by long-term warming, glacier retreat and geological instability.

‘Existential threat’

Much of Nepal’s hydropower infrastructure lies along steep river valleys fed by glaciers — terrain exposed to floods, landslides and cascading geological hazards.

“Powerhouses need to be moved higher up from the riverbeds to protect them against floods, we need better evacuation plans and stocked safehouses,” IPPAN’s Lama said.

“We should explore remotely operated systems so people are not stuck inside in case anything happens.”

The flooding has also renewed calls for diversifying the power mix in Nepal, which lacks coal or gas-fired generation capacity.

“Nepal’s electricity system, currently strained and heavily dependent on hydropower, could be made more robust through well-planned additions of solar electricity,” Germany’s development agency GIZ said in a 2024 report.

The challenge extends beyond Nepal.

Glaciers in the wider Himalayan and Hindu Kush ranges are a crucial water source for around 240 million people in the mountainous regions, as well as for another 1.65 billion people in the South Asian and Southeast Asian river valleys below.

Basanta Raj Adhikari, director at the Centre for Disaster Studies at Tribhuvan University, said the Himalayas must be monitored regionally for hotspots to develop early warning systems.

“I call it the fate of the Himalayan people,” he told AFP.

“It can happen anywhere in the world but the Himalayas are experiencing adverse impacts due to climate change and anthropogenic activity,” he said.

“We have to design climate-resilient infrastructures. That is our top priority because we are (facing) existential threat.”

item.title: The relationship between progress and cancer. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
That we're all at risk of dying from cancer is a good thing. No, really, I insist that this is true.
For what it is really saying is that we're all living long enough to die of cancer.
We're not, instead, dying young of infectious diseases, starvation, and war.
OK, fair enough, that's of small comfort to someone who has just received a cancer diagnosis. It's grossly unfair to those few who get struck down young.
From personal experience, a friend died of brain cancer at 16 years of age. My father, when announcing his own diagnosis at age 85, emailed us all to say: “I have lived long enough to get prostate cancer.”
Cancer is, barring those youthful tragedies, a disease of age and a life largely already lived. This may or may not be a comfort, but it's definitely a change.
This is the thing we need to keep in mind when we discuss things like the World Cancer Congress .
Yes, it is absolutely true that more of us die now of -- or even more of us will die of -- cancer than ever used to happen in the past.
But that's because in the past, most of us would already be dead.
We see some of the toll of those infectious diseases in the reports of the measles outbreak that has been occurring in Bangladesh. Hundreds dead. That's hundreds of individual tragedies. But it's worth reminding ourselves what it was like not so long ago.
Even in the richest countries two and three centuries back, it was expected that half of all children would die before puberty. About half of those -- so a quarter of all babies -- in that first and most delicate year of life. Then another half -- another quarter of all children -- from accidents and infections.
We would assume that a grieving parent today would have been most unlucky. Back then it was normal for this to happen several times in each family.
Once through those childhood diseases, lifespans were not too far off our own. Someone who reached 20 years of age could well expect to reach 60, for example. Probably the most dangerous thing was childbirth for women. Or war, of course.
What changed things was, in order, drains and drinkable water, followed by better nutrition, and only after that, the antibiotics and vaccines that deal with the infectious diseases themselves.
This is still ongoing, new vaccines arrive all the time. The HPV one has been around a bit more than a decade and already in the UK, cervical cancer among the under-30s has fallen to an effective zero.
It's possible to have great hope for the ongoing trials of mRNA vaccines -- the original intention was always for anti-cancer treatments. Covid was just a happenstance.
But the thing to grasp about high cancer rates in modern populations is that this isn't a result of modern life poisoning us and it's not even, despite what some will claim, because of our diet or exercise regimes. It's because, by any historical standard, we're rich these days.
You know that saying that the rich also have their problems? This is one of them, living long enough to get cancer.
We'd still like to beat cancer, sure we would. But that this is the problem we're worrying about now is evidence of how far we've already come.
Tim Worstall is a senior fellow at the Adam Smith Institute in London.

item.title: Bridging the last mile. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Two contrasting stories published in these pages highlight the starkly uneven reality of rural development in Bangladesh.
In Khulna’s Dakope upazila , the completion of the 661-metre Bhadra Bridge has finally connected seven isolated unions, ending decades of precarious ferry dependence for about 350,000 residents.
Meanwhile, in Tangail’s Bhuapur upazila , 10,000 citizens across seven villages along the Louhajang River still rely on a single, risky boat, waiting for a basic bridge that, 50 years later, is yet to be built.
These two narratives illustrate, above all else, a persistent flaw in our national planning.
While high-profile megaprojects absorb political capital and public attention, true equitable growth must be measured by last-mile connectivity.
A simple river crossing fundamentally transforms rural life: It allows, among others, children to reach schools safely, ensures critically ill patients access emergency healthcare without delay, and provides farmers direct access to bigger markets.
For marginalized communities, the lack of basic infrastructure is nothing if not a systemic failure that deprives them of fundamental socio-economic opportunities.
With that said, we must also contend with the sobering, familiar issue of exceeding costs and timelines for our infrastructure projects.
Originally tendered in 2016 for Tk 37.43 crore with a targeted completion date of early 2018, the Bhadra Bridge suffered multiple contractor defaults, administrative delays, and repeated timeline extensions. That the project ultimately dragged on for eight years and cost Tk 50.75 crore reflects an administration that is incompetent and unable to meet deadlines and budgets.
This culture of routine delay, fiscal inflation, and lax procurement oversight has plagued our public works sector for far too long. Inflated budgets and missed deadlines waste taxpayer money and delay vital public services, and we must have better discipline as a nation. That is non-negotiable.
Delivering infrastructure to the last mile is essential, but doing so on time and strictly within budget must become the standard for public governance.

item.title: A disgraceful assault. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The attack on the Radda MCH-FP Centre in Mirpur must be called out for what it was: A despicable act that sinks to the absolute lowest depths of moral bankruptcy.
Under the cover of darkness, a mob of over 200 masked men armed with hammers, sticks, and heavy excavators bound and gagged security guards before attempting to raze the healthcare facility to the ground.
That they looted essential medical equipment, ultrasound machinery, and cash from a centre that provided services primarily to disadvantaged and low-income people shows that, beyond being an illegal land grab, this was a barbaric, gutless act of aggression and brings profound national shame upon us all.
For five decades, the centre has served as a sanctuary for low-income families, providing essential care to over 400 underprivileged mothers, infants, and elderly patients every single day. To reduce such a vital community lifeline to a pile of rubble over a 10-katha real estate dispute is a heinous crime.
That perpetrators felt empowered to deploy heavy machinery in the heart of the capital at midnight reveals the magnitude of the impunity enjoyed by such criminals, making a mockery of law and order.
It goes without saying that this outrage demands an unyielding, zero-tolerance response. Excuses, bureaucratic delays, and political finger-pointing are completely unacceptable.
Every individual involved -- from the masked goons who wielded the hammers to those orchestrating the land grab under the guise of local associations -- must be prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law.
Failure to swiftly apprehend and try those responsible would signal a complete collapse of governance and a further invitation to mob rule. We expect the authorities concerned to demonstrate, through actions, that those who resort to such brutality will face uncompromising justice. Anything less is a betrayal.

item.title: Inflation seen slowing to 10.75pc in September. [ dawn ]
item.description:
KARACHI: Some stakeholders and analysts expect inflation in September to slow despite the high uncertainty caused by the ongoing Gulf war.

The financial sector expects oil prices to remain between $90 and $100 per barrel during the remaining days of September and in October.

However, the situation has once again changed after US President Donald Trump announced on Saturday that he had rejected Iran’s proposal for the Gulf war. Iran is now anticipating possible attacks from the US, raising concerns that oil prices could surge.

Analysts expect oil prices to remain around $100 per barrel if the war resumes. However, much will depend on the availability of oil supplies in the international market. Pakistan imports 70pc of its oil and gas requirements, making inflation highly sensitive to oil prices.

Stakeholders believe oil prices to hover around $100 per barrel

Pakistan’s official headline inflation rose sharply to 11.1pc year-on-year in August 2026, up from 9.2pc in July 2026.

According to a Topline Securities report, the Consumer Price Index (CPI) for September is expected to rise 10.25-10.75pc year-on-year, down from 11.1pc in August. This projection is slightly lower than the August figure, but does not represent a significant decline.

Petroleum prices have been rising daily in Pakistan and have now reached the highest level in the region. India increased petrol prices by 10pc, while Bangladesh reportedly jacked up by 16pc and Pakistan by over 50pc.

“It is not easy to assess the exact inflation figure for September as oil prices have been changing both internationally and locally. We can only expect slightly lower inflation, with a fear that it may remain close to last month’s level,” said S.S. Iqbal, a money market expert.

With inflation expected to remain at 10.25-10.75pc in September 2026, real interest rates are likely to stand at 75-125 basis points, lower than Pakistan’s historical average of 200-300 basis points, according to the Topline report.

Electricity, housing, food and construction costs have also witnessed increases, suggesting that inflation could come in above analysts’ expectations, particularly if the Gulf war continues for an extended period.

At the same time, Pakistan, Turkiye and Saudi Arabia are preparing to respond to a possible new conflict involving the Houthis and the kingdom, adding to uncertainty over oil prices and supplies. Any disruption could have a direct impact on Pakistan’s economy and inflation.

Pakistan’s foreign exchange reserves, currently exceeding $21.4 billion, may provide some cushion against higher oil import costs. However, they cannot prevent inflationary pressures from rising if the conflict continues and international energy prices remain elevated.

Published in Dawn, September 27th, 2026
